title: O Night, When Will the Lover's Morning Come?
intro: This is the best-known poem of Ali al-Husri, the blind poet of Kairouan: a praise poem of ninety-nine lines to Abu Abd al-Rahman Muhammad ibn Tahir, prince of Murcia, which its editors al-Marzuqi and al-Jilani think he wrote to answer a slander that he had insulted the prince in company. The recording gives its love prelude, the first twenty-three lines: a sleepless night, the beloved and his killing eyes, a plea for pity, and a claim of chaste love that, in the full poem, leads into the praise. The prelude became far better known than the poem it opens; Ibn Khallikan quoted two lines of it and stopped, saying “it is well known, so there is no need to give it”. Poets answered it in the same metre and rhyme, from Ibn Khallikan's friend al-Qamrawi down to Ahmad Shawqi's “Mudnaka jafahu marqaduhu”, and books of prosody quote its opening as an example of al-mutadarik in its quick, skipping form, the khabab.

translation: O night, the lover: when will his morning come?
Is it set for the Hour, when the dead rise?
1.sharh: He asks the night when the lover's morning will come, and whether it has been put off until the Day of Resurrection, so long does the night feel. The lover is the poet himself, spoken of as if he were someone else.

translation: The night's companions slept; he was kept awake
by grief at parting, which tossed him to and fro.
2.sharh: Everyone who sat up talking with him has gone to bed; he alone is kept awake by grief for the beloved who has left, and it gives him no rest. The Arabic sets the sleepers against the sleepless.

translation: The star wept for him and pitied him
for the way he watches it and waits for it to set.
3.sharh: He watches the star all night, waiting for it to set and bring the dawn, until the star itself weeps for him. If a star can pity him, the beloved has more reason to.

translation: He is in love with a gazelle, slender of waist,
whom fear of the talebearers drives away.
4.sharh: The beloved, a gazelle in grace, runs from him not out of dislike but for fear of the people who carry tales between lovers. As is usual in Arabic love poetry, the beloved is spoken of as masculine.

translation: My eyes set a snare for him
in sleep, and he was hard to catch.
5.sharh: Since the beloved will not come to him awake, he closes his eyes to catch a dream of him, as a hunter sets a trap. But he cannot sleep, so the dream never comes.

translation: It is wonder enough that I, who hunt the herd,
am taken captive by its most graceful one.
6.sharh: The hunter has become the prey: he who could catch any gazelle of the herd is himself made captive by the loveliest of them. In Arabic poetry a herd of gazelles stands for a company of beautiful women.

translation: An idol set up to bewitch:
I love it, but I do not worship it.
7.sharh: The beloved is like a statue of beauty set up to turn heads. The second half guards the image: his love stops short of worship, so the comparison cannot be taken for idolatry.

translation: Sober, though his mouth yields wine,
drunk in his glance, and wild with it.
8.sharh: The beloved has drunk nothing, yet his kiss tastes of wine; his glance droops like a drunkard's, yet it strikes as hard as a drunk who turns on his companions. Weakness in look and power in effect sit together in him.

translation: From his eye he draws a sword,
and drowsiness seems to sheathe it.
9.sharh: His glance is a sword drawn from the eye, and his heavy, half-closed lids are its sheath. Arabic poets prized that languor as the loveliest thing in an eye.

translation: With it he spills the blood of lovers,
and woe to the one who must bear that blood.
10.sharh: With that sword the beloved spills lovers' blood, and woe to whoever must answer for it, a hint at the beloved's guilt that the next line takes back. Others read it: woe to whoever that sword strikes.

translation: No: there is no guilt on one whose eyes
have killed, while his hand has not.
11.sharh: He takes back the charge at once: the beloved is not to blame, for his eyes did the killing, not his hand. To be killed by a glance is to fall in love, and no one is punished for his eyes.

translation: O you whose eyes deny my blood,
while your cheeks are flushed with it,
12.sharh: The beloved's eyes deny having shed his blood, but the rosy flush on the beloved's cheeks is that very blood, and it gives them away.

translation: your cheeks have confessed to my blood:
why then do your eyelids deny it?
13.sharh: The cheeks, red with his blood, have owned up; the eyes still deny it. He sets the beloved's face out like a court, with one witness confessing and the killer denying.

translation: I pray God to keep you from killing me,
and I believe you do not mean to.
14.sharh: He asks God to spare the beloved the sin of his death, and grants that it is not done on purpose. He clears the beloved even as he complains, and so prepares to plead.

translation: By God, grant the one who longs some sleep:
perhaps your phantom will bring him joy.
15.sharh: He begs for a little sleep so that he might see the beloved in a dream. What he really asks for is nearness, since a lover cannot sleep while his love is far.

translation: What harm would it do you to cure the wasting
of a lover who draws you near while you push him away?
16.sharh: It would cost the beloved nothing to heal him. He keeps drawing the beloved close in longing; the beloved keeps him at a distance.

translation: Your love has left him no breath of life:
let those who visit the sick weep for him.
17.sharh: Love has left him nothing to live on. Those who come to sit with him in his sickness may as well begin to mourn, as visitors do when the end is near.

translation: Tomorrow or the day after, he will die:
is there a glance he can take with him?
18.sharh: He will be dead within a day or two. All he asks now is one look at the beloved to take with him, as a traveller takes provisions for the road.

translation: O people of longing, we are choking
on tears whose rosy flood spills over.
19.sharh: He calls on his fellow lovers: we are choking, he says, on tears that run red, as if tinged with blood. Others take the rosy thing to be the eye or cheek, reddened by weeping. Longing and choking, shawq and sharaq, chime in Arabic.

translation: The one who longs would love to meet you,
and the turns of time keep him away.
20.sharh: The lover wants nothing more than to be with his loved ones, but circumstance keeps carrying him off, again and again.

translation: How sweet union is, how pleasant,
were it not that the days spoil it
21.sharh: Union with the beloved would be the sweetest thing there is, if only the days did not keep souring it. The sentence runs on into the next line, which says how.

translation: with parting and desertion. Ah,
my poor heart: how does it hold out?
22.sharh: The days spoil it with partings and coldness. He cries out over his own heart, amazed that it can bear so much.

translation: Of all who love, I am the most chaste;
others spoil love with what is wrong.
23.sharh: In love he keeps within what is lawful, while others corrupt it with licence. Here the love prelude ends; in the full poem the next line turns to the praise of the prince.

1.1.3.head: الصَّبّ
1.1.3.meaning: Sabb: a lover consumed by longing.

1.2.1-2.meaning: “The rising of the Hour”: the Day of Resurrection.

2.1.2.head: السُّمّار
2.1.2.meaning: Summar: friends who sit up at night talking.

3.2.2.head: رَعى
3.2.2.meaning: Watches the star through the night, waiting for it to set.

4.2.2.head: الواشي
4.2.2.meaning: Talebearers, who carry gossip between lovers to part them.

6.2.1.head: السِّرب
6.2.1.meaning: Sirb: a herd of gazelles; here, a company of beautiful women.

6.2.3.head: أَغيَد
6.2.3.meaning: Aghyad: soft and supple, with a swaying neck.

8.1.3.meaning: Fruit, what is picked: his mouth yields wine.

8.2.3.head: مُعَربِد
8.2.3.meaning: Mu'arbid: a drunk who turns violent on his companions.

9.1.1.head: نَضا
9.1.1.meaning: Draws a sword from its sheath.

10.2.3.head: تَقَلَّدَ
10.2.3.meaning: Girds on a sword; also, takes a burden on oneself. Here, bears the guilt of the blood, or wears the sword.

12.1.3.head: جَحَدَ
12.1.3.meaning: Denied what it knew to be true. Some sources have safakat, “shed”.

12.2.3.head: تَوَرُّد
12.2.3.meaning: A rosy flush, the colour of the rose (ward).

15.2.2.head: خَيال
15.2.2.meaning: Khayal: the beloved's phantom, seen in dreams.

17.1.5.head: رَمَق
17.1.5.meaning: Ramaq: the last breath of life.

17.2.3.head: عُوَّد
17.2.3.meaning: Uwwad: those who visit the sick.

18.2.4.head: تَزَوَّدَ
18.2.4.meaning: Takes as provisions for a journey; here, the journey of death.

19.1.5.head: شَرَق
19.1.5.meaning: Sharaq: choking on water or tears.

19.2.3.head: مُوَرَّد
19.2.3.meaning: Muwarrad: rose-tinted; the tears red with blood. Some prints have mawriduhu, “its spring”, which does not scan.

20.2.1.head: ظُروف
20.2.1.meaning: Circumstances. Zahr al-Adab has wa-surufu, “the blows of fortune”.

22.2.1.head: فُؤاد
22.2.1.meaning: “O for my heart”: a cry of wonder and appeal.
